name: .22 Short-Long
description:
The .22 Short-Long is the oldest surviving rimfire cartridge still in mass production in GLMZ 2200, a near-unchanged descendant of the nineteenth-century .22 Short and Long Rifle merged into a single unified spec by Slagworks Industrial in 2141 to reduce manufacturing overhead. The consolidation was controversial — purists and collectors still argue about the original distinction — but practically speaking, the round that emerged is a cheap, low-recoil, low-noise cartridge that loads in virtually anything chambered for either ancestor. Brass-cased versions still outnumber caseless by a wide margin, partly because the tooling to produce them never changed and partly because Tier 1 reloaders can refurbish spent brass with minimal equipment.

In GLMZ 2200, the .22 Short-Long is the round of the dispossessed. Shelf workers keep battered pocket pistols loaded with it. Excluded zone survivors use it in cobbled-together single-shots and improvised revolvers because the cases are everywhere — spilled from torn bags on the freight docks, sold loose by the handful at gray market stalls in the Underward. It is not a fight-stopper. Everyone knows it is not a fight-stopper. But it is quiet, it is available, and at close range in a desperate moment, it has ended enough lives that no one laughs at it out loud.
compatibility_note: Compatible with any firearm chambered for legacy .22 Short, .22 Long, or .22 Long Rifle, as well as unified .22 Short-Long spec weapons. Common in Slagworks-manufactured pocket pistols, survival rifles, and improvised Excluded-zone firearms. Many bolt-action and semi-auto rimfire platforms accept it without modification.
reliability_note: Among the most reliable cartridges in GLMZ by sheer virtue of age and simplicity. Rimfire ignition is marginally less consistent than centerfire in extreme cold or after prolonged moisture exposure, but modern Slagworks production brass has largely addressed this. Reloaded or salvage brass is less predictable. No battery, no optic, no containment — it fires when struck, period.
